Amber faces the sea. The paths through Arden lead toward its harbor. Corwin knows [every road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Chronicles_of_Amber) that ends at the quay, and he walks the last mile slowly, counting lanterns as they wake along the wall.

The city rises in terraces above the water. Pale towers catch the first light while the lower streets still hold the night. Bakers open their doors before the bells, and the smell of warm bread drifts down the stairs toward the fish market, where the boats are already unloading.

From the garden path you can see the whole bay. Cypress trees stand along the wall like a quiet guard. Below them the roofs step down to the harbor, red tile after red tile, until the last house leans over the water and its windows shine with the color of the morning sea.

Arden begins where the stone road ends. The forest is older than the city and keeps its own hours. Light falls through the leaves in long gold bars, and the stream under the old bridge runs clear and cold. Travelers who cross it at dawn say that the water remembers every step taken on the way to [Amber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Princes_in_Amber).

By noon the courtyard is full of voices. The fountain throws its thin silver arc into the basin, and children run between the columns. Flowering trees lean over the arches, and their petals settle on the warm stones. Someone tunes a lute in the shade, and the first slow notes rise with the pigeons.

The coast road is best in autumn. The cliffs turn copper and rust, and the wind brings the smell of salt and dry grass. Far below, the sea folds itself against the rocks. A rider on that road sees the towers long before the gates, small and bright against the edge of the sky.

Evening comes to the harbor first. The masts stand dark against the last light, and the water takes the color of the lamps. Sailors coil their ropes and talk about the weather beyond the headland. Above them the terraces glow one by one, as if the city were lighting a path for the moon.

At night the lanterns keep watch. The moon stands over the towers and lays a white road across the bay. The bridges hold their reflections without a ripple. Somewhere a door closes, a dog answers another dog, and then the only sound is the tide moving under the quay.

The library stands behind the high garden. Its shelves climb into the dark, and the ladders creak like old ships. Maps of Arden hang beside charts of the bay, each one drawn by a different hand. A reader may spend a winter there and still not reach the end of a single aisle.

Market day fills the lower square with color. Baskets of pears and figs stand beside bolts of blue cloth. A juggler works the corner by the well, and the crowd laughs when he drops nothing at all. By the third bell the stalls are half empty and the stones are bright with spilled water.

Rain in Amber is a gentle thing. It comes in from the sea in a grey curtain and washes the terraces clean. The gutters sing, the gardens darken, and the towers vanish for an hour into the cloud. Then the wind turns, the light returns, and every roof shines like a new coin.

The watch changes at the fourth bell. Guards trade a few quiet words at the gate and look once toward the forest road. Nothing moves there but the fog. They bank the fire, shoulder their cloaks, and begin the slow walk along the wall, from the harbor tower to the garden stair.

The lighthouse at the end of the mole is the oldest thing in the harbor. Its keeper trims the lamp at dusk and writes the names of passing ships in a narrow book. On clear nights the beam reaches the far headland, and sailors far out at sea turn their bows toward it and know that they are nearly home.

Winter is short on this coast. Snow rests on the highest roofs for a week and is gone. The fishermen mend their nets by the stove, and the children wait for the first warm day. When it comes, the whole city opens its shutters at once, and the sea is suddenly full of sails.

Those who leave Amber carry its light with them. They remember the garden above the harbor, the cool shade of Arden, the fountain in the courtyard and the long road by the sea. And when they return, the city greets them the same way: quietly, with open gates and a lamp in every window.
